clauses.reason: Whole order (single operative paragraph, offsets 0-684 of the held text jobs/app-executive-orders/output/texts/executive-order-8413-exemption-hubert-k-bishop-from-compulsory-retirement-for-age.txt): signed May 18, 1940. The recital finds that the public interest requires that the employee be exempted from compulsory retirement for age for a period of one year, and the operative sentence, under section 204 of the act of June 30, 1932 (47 Stat. 382, 404), exempts Hubert K. Bishop from compulsory retirement for age for a period of one year ending June 30 of a year the held text prints as 1041 (read as 1941). That exemption is the order's only command and it carries its own fixed term. First end: the order's own stated end, June 30 of the year printed 1041 and read as 1941 (operative sentence: "for a period of one year ending June 30, 1041."). The stated date is recorded inclusive (the exemption runs through the end of June 30, 1941); the exclusive reading, under which it ends when June 30, 1941 begins, is the alternative. The date is the end of the stated term, not a record of separation or death; no such record is held. The held text prints the end year as 1041, an evident misprint (the order is dated May 18, 1940, so an exemption ending in 1041 is impossible); the one-year period, the recital that the employee reaches retirement age in June 1940, and EO 8810 (below) support June 30, 1941. Later event, not an end: Executive Order 8810, signed June 30, 1941, further exempts the same person; its recital names this order ("by Executive Order No. 8413 of May 18, 1940") and its operative sentence runs "ending June 30, 1942". Like this order it has no effective-date wording, so I read it as effective on signing. The date recorded is June 30, 1941; EO 8810 recites a one-year exemption by this order and further exempts the employee for a year ending June 30, 1942, which fits an end of June 30, 1941.

savings.reason: The exemption let Hubert K. Bishop remain in service past the retirement age that would otherwise have required automatic separation; service rendered while the exemption ran is an accrued effect that remains after the stated end date. The order says nothing about any status, right or duty after June 30, 1941, so no independent continuing command or residual obligation of this order survives its stated term. Later service under the further exemption came from a separate order, not from this one.
